name: Refugios de la Guerra Civil, Almería (air-raid shelters)
text: Almería, the Republic's main port on the south-east coast, was bombed repeatedly from the air and the sea — the local memory association counts 57 raids. The worst single attack came at dawn on 31 May 1937, when the German cruiser Admiral Scheer and four destroyers shelled the city in reprisal for a Republican air attack on the cruiser Deutschland off Ibiza; around 19–20 civilians died. In response the city dug one of Europe's largest civilian shelter networks: more than 4 km of galleries about 9 m underground, built 1936–38 for some 40,000 people, with an operating theatre and store rooms. The city was also swollen by refugees from the fall of Málaga in February 1937.
look: About 1 km of restored galleries, the underground operating theatre, a food store and an introductory video; entrance kiosk on Plaza Manuel Pérez García.
plan: Guided visits only (in Spanish, c. 1 hour), Tuesday–Sunday mornings plus Friday–Saturday evenings; book at the tourist office, the kiosk or by phone (950 268 696). Small fee.
disputed: Capacity and number of raids vary between sources (40,000 people is the usual figure; the memorial association says over 75% of the population). Deaths in the 31 May 1937 bombardment are given as 19–20.

name: Barranco de Víznar (mass graves, Place of Memory)
text: After the military rising took Granada in July 1936, the rebel civil government organised the execution of Republican supporters, trade unionists, teachers and politicians. Many were taken at night from La Colonia, a house in Víznar used as a holding point, and shot in this pine-covered ravine beside the Víznar–Alfacar road, where they were buried in pits and natural hollows. Killings continued into the post-war years. University of Granada excavations since the 2010s have located some 29 graves and recovered the remains of 166 people, a few of them since identified by DNA. The ravine is an official Andalusian Place of Memory, and for many it stands for all the victims of the repression in Granada.
look: A path through the pines to excavated and marked graves, a stone monolith inscribed 'Todos eran Lorca' (2002) and a stone gallery with metal plaques bearing victims' names.
plan: Open access and free, on the GR-3101 between Víznar and Alfacar; roadside parking. A night poetry vigil is held each 18–19 August. Combine with Alfacar (1 km west).
disputed: The total number of people killed and buried at Víznar–Alfacar is unknown; estimates run from hundreds to over a thousand. Exhumation counts rise with each campaign.

name: Parque Federico García Lorca, Alfacar (Fuente Grande)
text: Federico García Lorca, Spain's best-known poet and dramatist, was arrested in Granada on 16 August 1936 and shot in the early hours near the Fuente Grande spring, with the schoolteacher Dióscoro Galindo and the banderilleros Francisco Galadí and Joaquín Arcollas. Lorca was a Republican sympathiser but not a party member; his killing by the rebel authorities became a worldwide symbol of the war's repression. The provincial council opened this park in 1986 on the spot then believed to be the grave, beside an old olive tree. Excavations in late 2009 found no human remains there, and the location of Lorca's body remains unknown.
look: A landscaped park with fountains and walls bearing lines of Lorca's poetry, a monolith dedicated 'to Federico García Lorca and all victims of the Civil War' and the olive tree long taken as the execution spot.
plan: Open access, free, on the GR-3101 above Alfacar. A commemorative evening of music and readings is held each 18 August.
disputed: The date of Lorca's death is given as 17, 18 or 19 August 1936, and the exact site and his grave are unknown; the 2009 dig at the olive tree found nothing.

name: Huerta de San Vicente (García Lorca house-museum), Granada
text: The García Lorca family's summer home from 1926 to 1936, where the poet wrote much of Blood Wedding and Yerma. Lorca came here from Madrid in July 1936, days before the rising. When the military seized Granada, the house was searched; his brother-in-law Manuel Fernández-Montesinos, the Socialist mayor, was arrested and shot in August. Lorca took refuge in the house of the Rosales family, Falangists and friends, but was arrested there on 16 August and killed days later near Alfacar. The family sold the house to the city in 1985 and it opened as a museum in 1995. It is the best place to understand Lorca the writer before visiting the sites of his death.
look: The whitewashed farmhouse, largely unchanged, with family furniture, Lorca's desk and piano, drawings and documents, in the Parque García Lorca.
plan: Guided visits only, in small groups; closed Mondays. Book ahead in summer; small fee (free day weekly). Official site: huertadesanvicente.com.

name: Paseo de los Canadienses / Peñón del Cuervo — 'La Desbandá' memorial, Málaga
text: When Nationalist and Italian CTV forces took Málaga on 8 February 1937, a huge column of civilians and militiamen fled east along the only coast road towards Almería, some 200 km away. On the road they were shelled from the sea by the cruisers Canarias, Almirante Cervera and Baleares and attacked from the air; many also died of exhaustion or drowned at river crossings. The Canadian surgeon Norman Bethune, with Hazen Sise and Thomas Worsley, drove his blood-transfusion truck along the road ferrying the weakest to Almería, and his pamphlet made the 'Desbandá' known abroad. This seafront walk, opened on 7 February 2006, marks the start of the route and honours Bethune and the aid of the Canadian people.
look: A seafront promenade at the Peñón del Cuervo cove on the old coast road east of Málaga, with a plaque to Bethune and the Canadian aid; the N-340 coast road the refugees followed runs alongside.
plan: Open access, free; bus or car along the N-340 towards Rincón de la Victoria. The 'La Desbandá' association runs a commemorative walk to Almería each February.
disputed: Death toll unknown. Figures of 3,000–5,000 dead (some claims far higher) are widely quoted; historians such as Antonio Nadal think the true figure may be significantly lower. Estimates of the number fleeing run from about 100,000 to nearly 300,000 (Junta de Andalucía).

name: Santuario de la Virgen de la Cabeza (1936–37 siege), Andújar
text: In September 1936 about 250 Civil Guards, some Falangists and around 1,000 of their family members and civilians from Jaén province shut themselves into this hilltop sanctuary in the Sierra Morena, deep inside Republican territory. Captain Santiago Cortés deposed the commander who favoured surrender and held out for more than seven months, supplied by Nationalist aircraft dropping food and medicine. A Nationalist relief offensive stalled at Lopera in December. Republican forces under Lt. Col. García Vallejo and Maj. Martínez Cartón, eventually 6,000 or more men, stormed the ruins on 1 May 1937; Cortés was mortally wounded and the survivors surrendered. Franco's regime made the siege a heroic legend, rather like the Alcázar of Toledo.
look: The sanctuary, rebuilt after its destruction in the siege, on its granite hilltop; a 22 m monument of 1965 with a bronze Angel of Victory lifting a fallen defender; relics including Cortés's Laureate Cross.
plan: Open daily as a working shrine; 32 km north of Andújar by the J-5010 through the Sierra de Andújar park. Avoid the huge Romería on the last weekend of April unless you want the pilgrimage.
disputed: The monument and its inscriptions reflect the Francoist narrative and are debated under Spain's democratic memory laws. Numbers of besiegers are given as 6,000–12,000.

name: Lopera — battlefield and Jardín de los Poetas Ingleses (Cornford & Fox)
text: On Christmas Day 1936 Nationalist troops took Lopera during their 'olive offensive' towards Andújar. The Republic threw in the newly formed XIV International Brigade under General 'Walter' (Karol Świerczewski) — French, Belgian, British and Irish volunteers with little training, no telephones and scant artillery or air support. Their attacks on the hills around the town, including the Cerro del Calvario, were beaten off by requetés and Moroccan Regulares. The English-speaking No. 1 Company lost heavily: the poet John Cornford, 21, a great-grandson of Charles Darwin, and the novelist Ralph Fox were killed. The front then settled here until 1939, leaving machine-gun nests, trenches and bunkers. It was the Brigades' last action in Andalusia.
look: In town, the Jardín de los Poetas Ingleses with a monolith and a bronze relief of Cornford by Frank Casey (2019); outside, two concrete Nationalist machine-gun nests near the Arroyo Salado bridge (2.5 km out), traces of Republican trenches on the Cerro de las Esperillas and an anti-tank bunker at Valcargado.
plan: Ask at the town hall (lopera.es) for a map of the vestiges; the machine-gun nests are signed off the road near the Puente del Arroyo Salado. A re-enactment is held in late May some years.
disputed: Losses vary widely: about 800 Brigade casualties incl. 300 dead (Wikipedia) vs about 500 casualties (Junta). Of the British/Irish company, 78 of 145 are said to have been lost; the IBMT counts 13 British and Irish dead. Fox's death is dated 27 or 28 December.

name: Parque de la Memoria 'Málaga 1937', Torre del Mar
text: Torre del Mar, about 30 km east of Málaga, was where refugees fleeing along the coast road met those coming down from the villages of the Axarquía during the exodus of February 1937. In 2007 the town opened this memorial garden by the artist Rogelio López Cuenca and architect Santiago Cirugeda, deliberately not a monument but a place to meet. It was among the first sites declared a Place of Memory in Andalusia (2013), and the annual commemoration of the Desbandá has been held here since 2005. Nearby, in Río Seco, a small square is named after Norman Bethune.
look: A plaque reading 'MÁLAGA 1937 / NUNCA MÁS' split by a crack tracing the coast to Almería, almond trees that flower each February, and more than 400 plaques with survivors' names written in their own hand.
plan: Open access, next to the bus station and the Mancomunidad de la Axarquía building in Torre del Mar. Combine with the Peñón del Cuervo memorial on the way from Málaga.
disputed: Death toll of the Desbandá is disputed (see Paseo de los Canadienses entry).

name: Panteón de la Memoria, Cementerio de San Rafael, Málaga
text: After Málaga fell in February 1937, military courts and summary shootings killed thousands of Republican supporters, many against the wall of the old San Rafael cemetery. Their bodies were thrown into mass graves there. Between 2006 and 2009 archaeologists exhumed 2,840 bodies — one of the largest Civil War grave excavations in Spain. The cemetery has since been turned into a park and the remains placed in a memorial pantheon, inaugurated on 11 January 2014. Málaga had also seen heavy repression in the Republican zone in the first months of the war, before the city fell; the two waves of killing should be understood together.
look: A park on the site of the former cemetery with the Panteón de la Memoria, a monument holding the recovered remains, and walls of victims' names.
plan: Camino de San Rafael, in the Carretera de Cádiz district west of the centre; open during park hours, free.
disputed: Total victims of the Nationalist repression in Málaga are variously estimated at around 4,000 or more; killings in the Republican zone in Málaga (July 1936–Feb 1937) are estimated at around 2,500. Figures vary by historian.

name: Cementerio de San Fernando — Pico Reja mass grave, Seville
text: General Gonzalo Queipo de Llano seized Seville on 18 July 1936, crushing working-class resistance in Triana and La Macarena and broadcasting nightly radio speeches from Unión Radio that threatened opponents with death. The repression that followed killed thousands in the city. Many were buried in Pico Reja, a mass grave in the municipal cemetery of San Fernando. Among them is probably Blas Infante, the 'father of Andalusian nationalism', shot on 11 August 1936 at km 4 of the Carmona road. Excavations begun in 2020 are one of the largest in Spain.
look: The municipal cemetery with the excavated Pico Reja area and memorial markers; the exhumation site itself may be fenced.
plan: Cemetery open daily; ask at the entrance for the Pico Reja area. For Infante, his house in Coria del Río is now the Museum of Andalusian Autonomy.
disputed: Number of dead in Pico Reja and of Seville's repression overall is disputed; identification of Infante's remains had not been confirmed at time of writing.

name: Refugio antiaéreo de Villanueva de Córdoba
text: Villanueva de Córdoba lay in the Republican-held north of Córdoba province, close to the front around Pozoblanco. In March–April 1937 Queipo de Llano's forces tried to break through to the Almadén mercury mines and were stopped at Pozoblanco by Republican forces under Joaquín Pérez Salas and others; the front then stayed close by until the end of the war. Nationalist aircraft bombed the towns of the area, and in 1937 Villanueva built an underground shelter beneath its main square. It is one of the declared Places of Democratic Memory in Andalusia.
look: An underground shelter beneath the Plaza de España.
plan: Visits by arrangement; ask at the town hall or tourist office in the Plaza de España.

name: Espejo — site of Capa's 'Falling Soldier'
text: Robert Capa's photograph of a militiaman falling backwards, published in Vu on 23 September 1936 and in Life in 1937, became the defining image of the war. For decades it was said to show the anarchist Federico Borrell García killed at Cerro Muriano, north of Córdoba, on 5 September 1936. In 2009 José Manuel Susperregui matched the skyline to the outskirts of Espejo, about 50 km away, where the front was quiet at the time; many now think the picture was staged or taken during an exercise. Espejo shows how the Córdoba front lines ran through open countryside in the first summer.
look: The open, rolling farmland around Espejo, whose skyline was matched to the photographs; no memorial or marker is known.
plan: Drive around the outskirts of Espejo with a copy of the photograph; the fields are private farmland, so view from tracks.
disputed: Location (Cerro Muriano vs Espejo), identity of the soldier and whether the scene was staged are all disputed.

name: Puente Viejo de Maro (Desbandá crossing), Nerja
text: The old bridge over the Barranco de Maro, east of Nerja, carried the coast road used by the refugees fleeing Málaga in February 1937. Nearby the road was shelled from the sea, and at the Río de la Miel crossing many were killed. In Nerja itself, evacuation buses with children were bombed. The bridge was declared a Place of Democratic Memory in 2013.
look: The old stone bridge over the ravine on the old coast road near Maro, with a memorial plaque.
plan: Park in Maro and walk; about 3 km east of Nerja.
disputed: Numbers killed on this stretch are unknown.

name: Puerto de Almería & Parque de las Almadrabillas
text: Almería's harbour was the arrival point for tens of thousands of refugees from Málaga in February 1937, and the target of the German naval bombardment of 31 May 1937. After the war, many Andalusian Republican exiles who had fled to France were captured by the Germans in 1940 and sent to Mauthausen; of about 1,500 who passed through the camp only about 500 survived. The memorial in the Parque de las Almadrabillas by the port remembers them.
look: The harbour front and the memorial to the Mauthausen deportees in the Almadrabillas park.
plan: 10 minutes' walk from the shelters; open access.
disputed: Numbers of Andalusian deportees to Mauthausen vary between sources.

name: Fuerte de Carchuna and the Motril front, Granada coast
text: After the fall of Málaga the front on the Granada coast stabilised between Motril (Nationalist) and the Republican zone to the east, and stayed there until 1939. On 23 May 1938 a Republican guerrilla unit landed by boat and attacked the fort of Carchuna, where prisoners (mostly Asturian miners) were held as forced labourers; 308 escaped to the Republican lines. It was one of the most successful special operations of the war. Trenches of the static front survive nearby.
look: The 18th-century coastal fort of Carchuna and remains of the front-line trenches.
plan: Fort seen from the outside by the N-340; trenches on the nearby hills — ask locally.
disputed: Number freed is given as around 300; 308 per the La Desbandá association.

name: Tablada airfield (Army of Africa airlift), Seville
coord_source: none verified (estimate; en.wikipedia Tablada_Air_Base redirects to Seville Airport)
text: With the Republican navy blocking the Strait, Franco's Army of Africa was stuck in Morocco. From late July 1936 German Junkers Ju 52 and Italian Savoia-Marchetti transports flew legionnaires and Regulares from Tetuán to Seville — the first large military airlift in history, landing mainly at Tablada and at Jerez. The troops then marched north to Badajoz and Madrid. The airfield was a military base and aviation school afterwards.
look: A military base; only its perimeter can be seen.
disputed: Numbers flown across are given differently in sources.
